resources.title: Physics equation sheet
resources.summary: All 35 equations on AQA's Physics equation sheet, grouped by topic, with what every symbol stands for and its unit. The six marked HT are for Higher tier papers only.
resources.statusNote: This page follows AQA's sheet for the June 2027 exams, which prints all 35 equations. You will be given the same sheet in exams from 2028. Ofqual, the exams regulator for England, decided this on 5 May 2026. The sheet stays unchanged, and these are equations you must be able to use and apply but are "not required to memorise". AQA must publish each year's sheet by 1 September of the year before. No question will ask you just to copy an equation down. The marks are for choosing the right equation, rearranging it and using the right units.

sources.name: Ofqual: formulae and equation sheets from 2028

applications.title: Car crash safety
applications.body: Crumple zones and airbags make the stop take longer. With $F = \dfrac{m\,\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, the same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force. A 70 kg passenger slowing from 15 m/s to rest in 0.05 s feels $\dfrac{70 \times 15}{0.05} = 21\,000$ N. Stretch the stop to 0.5 s and the force is $\dfrac{70 \times 15}{0.5} = 2100$ N, ten times smaller.

applications.title: Your electricity bill
applications.body: A 2 kW kettle is used for 15 minutes in total over a day. In the sheet's units, $E = P\,t = 2000 \times 900 = 1\,800\,000$ J. Bills use a bigger unit of energy, the kilowatt-hour (kWh): power in kW times time in hours, so $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$ kWh. The bill is that number times the price per kilowatt-hour.

applications.title: Wi-Fi and radio
applications.body: A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi signal has a frequency of $2.4 \times 10^9$ Hz and travels at $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, so $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{2.4 \times 10^9} = 0.125$ m. That is 12.5 cm, which sets the size of the aerial inside a router.

applications.title: Charging a phone
applications.body: A phone charger has a small transformer inside it. Suppose a transformer stepped 230 V mains straight down to 5 V. Then $\dfrac{n_p}{n_s} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{230}{5} = 46$, so the primary coil needs 46 turns for every 1 turn on the secondary. A real charger has extra parts too, because a battery needs direct current and a transformer only works with alternating current.

items.name: Kinetic energy
items.symbols: $E_k$ kinetic energy (J), $m$ mass (kg), $v$ speed (m/s)

items.name: Elastic potential energy
items.symbols: $E_e$ elastic potential energy (J), $k$ spring constant (N/m), $e$ extension (m). Only works up to the limit of proportionality: the point where the spring stops stretching in step with the force.

items.name: Gravitational potential energy
items.symbols: $E_p$ gravitational potential energy (J), $m$ mass (kg), $g$ gravitational field strength (N/kg), $h$ height (m). The value of $g$ is given in the question.

items.name: Change in thermal energy
items.symbols: $\Delta E$ change in thermal energy (J), $m$ mass (kg), $c$ specific heat capacity (J/kg °C), $\Delta\theta$ temperature change (°C). $c$ is the energy needed to warm 1 kg by 1 °C.

items.name: Power from energy
items.symbols: $P$ power (W), $E$ energy transferred (J), $t$ time (s)

items.name: Power from work
items.symbols: $P$ power (W), $W$ work done (J), $t$ time (s)

items.name: Efficiency from energy
items.symbols: A fraction or a percentage, with no unit. The sheet says "useful output energy transfer" over "total input energy transfer". Example: a motor takes in 200 J and gives out 150 J usefully. Efficiency $= \dfrac{150}{200} = 0.75$, or 75%.

items.name: Efficiency from power
items.symbols: No unit. Never more than 1, or 100%.

items.name: Charge flow
items.symbols: $Q$ charge (C), $I$ current (A), $t$ time (s)

items.name: Potential difference
items.symbols: $V$ potential difference (V), $I$ current (A), $R$ resistance (Ω)

items.name: Power from potential difference and current
items.symbols: $P$ power (W), $V$ potential difference (V), $I$ current (A)

items.name: Power from current and resistance
items.symbols: $P$ power (W), $I$ current (A), $R$ resistance (Ω). Square the current first, then multiply. Example: $I = 3$ A and $R = 10$ Ω give $P = 3^2 \times 10 = 9 \times 10 = 90$ W.

items.name: Energy from power
items.symbols: $E$ energy transferred (J), $P$ power (W), $t$ time (s)

items.name: Energy from charge
items.symbols: $E$ energy transferred (J), $Q$ charge flow (C), $V$ potential difference (V)

items.name: Density
items.symbols: $\rho$ density (kg/m³), $m$ mass (kg), $V$ volume (m³)

items.name: Change of state
items.symbols: $E$ energy (J), $m$ mass (kg), $L$ specific latent heat (J/kg). $L$ is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg. The temperature stays the same while the state changes: the energy changes the internal energy store instead.

items.name: Gas pressure and volume
items.symbols: $p$ pressure (Pa), $V$ volume (m³). For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. Before and after a change the product is the same: $p_1V_1 = p_2V_2$. Example: a gas at 100 000 Pa fills 0.30 m³. Squeezed to 0.10 m³, $p_2 = \dfrac{100\,000 \times 0.30}{0.10} = 300\,000$ Pa.

items.name: Weight
items.symbols: $W$ weight (N), $m$ mass (kg), $g$ gravitational field strength (N/kg)

items.name: Work done
items.symbols: $W$ work done (J), $F$ force (N), $s$ distance along the line of the force (m)

items.name: Force on a spring
items.symbols: $F$ force (N), $k$ spring constant (N/m), $e$ extension (m)

items.name: Moment
items.symbols: $M$ moment (N m), $F$ force (N), $d$ perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m)

items.name: Pressure
items.symbols: $p$ pressure (Pa), $F$ force at right angles to the surface (N), $A$ area (m²)

items.name: Pressure in a liquid
items.symbols: $p$ pressure (Pa), $h$ height of the column (m), $\rho$ density of the liquid (kg/m³), $g$ gravitational field strength (N/kg)

items.name: Distance
items.symbols: $s$ distance (m), $v$ speed (m/s), $t$ time (s)

items.name: Acceleration
items.symbols: $a$ acceleration (m/s²), $\Delta v$ change in velocity (m/s), $t$ time taken (s)

items.name: Uniform acceleration
items.symbols: $v$ final velocity (m/s), $u$ initial velocity (m/s), $a$ acceleration (m/s²), $s$ distance (m). Example: a car brakes from 20 m/s to rest in 50 m. $0^2 - 20^2 = 2 \times a \times 50$, so $a = \dfrac{-400}{100} = -4$ m/s². The minus sign means it is slowing down.

items.name: Resultant force
items.symbols: $F$ resultant force (N), $m$ mass (kg), $a$ acceleration (m/s²)

items.name: Momentum
items.symbols: $p$ momentum (kg m/s), $m$ mass (kg), $v$ velocity (m/s)

items.name: Force and change in momentum
items.symbols: $F$ force (N), $m$ mass (kg), $\Delta v$ change in velocity (m/s), $\Delta t$ time taken (s). $m\,\Delta v$ is the change in momentum (kg m/s).

items.name: Period
items.symbols: $T$ period (s), $f$ frequency (Hz)

items.name: Wave speed
items.symbols: $v$ wave speed (m/s), $f$ frequency (Hz), $\lambda$ wavelength (m)

items.name: Magnification
items.symbols: A ratio, so no unit. Measure both heights in the same unit, mm or cm. Example: an image 30 mm tall of an object 6 mm tall has magnification $\dfrac{30}{6} = 5$.

items.name: Force on a conductor
items.symbols: $F$ force (N), $B$ magnetic flux density (T), $I$ current (A), $l$ length of conductor in the field (m). Only when the conductor is at right angles to the field.

items.name: Transformer turns
items.symbols: $V$ potential difference (V), $n$ number of turns, $p$ primary coil, $s$ secondary coil

items.name: Transformer power
items.symbols: $V_p$ and $I_p$ are the potential difference (V) and current (A) in the primary coil. $V_s$ and $I_s$ are the same for the secondary coil. Each side is a power in watts: power in equals power out, for a transformer that is 100% efficient.

blocks.body: **One letter, two jobs.** $W$ is weight in $W = m\,g$ but work done in $W = F\,s$. $p$ is pressure in $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$ but momentum in $p = m\,v$. $V$ is potential difference in $V = I\,R$ but volume in $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$. The sign $\Delta$ (delta) means "change in". Check the name of the equation to see which meaning is in use.

resources.title: SI units and prefixes
resources.summary: The unit every quantity on the equation sheet is measured in, and the prefixes from nano to tera, with how to convert between them.

applications.title: Reading a plug-in charger
applications.body: A charger labelled 5 V, 2000 mA gives $2000 \times 10^{-3} = 2$ A, so its power is $P = V\,I = 10$ W.

applications.title: Light and the size of atoms
applications.body: Green light has a wavelength of about 500 nm, which is $500 \times 10^{-9} = 5 \times 10^{-7}$ m. An atom has a radius of about $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. The wavelength is $\dfrac{5 \times 10^{-7}}{1 \times 10^{-10}} = 5000$ times bigger.

applications.title: Power stations
applications.body: A large power station is rated at about 2 GW, which is $2 \times 10^9$ W. That would run a million 2 kW kettles at once: $\dfrac{2 \times 10^9}{2 \times 10^3} = 10^6$.

blocks.title: Quantities and their units
rows: joule per kilogram per degree Celsius
blocks.note: Mass is in kilograms, not grams, and time in seconds, not minutes or hours: convert before you substitute. 250 g is $250 \div 1000 = 0.25$ kg. 5 minutes is $5 \times 60 = 300$ s. 50 cm² is $50 \div 10\,000 = 0.005$ m². A density of 2.7 g/cm³ is $2.7 \times 1000 = 2700$ kg/m³.

blocks.title: Prefixes
blocks.note: To go from a prefixed unit to the plain unit, multiply by the power of ten: 250 mA is $250 \times 10^{-3} = 0.25$ A. To go back, divide: 0.002 A is $0.002 \div 10^{-3} = 2$ mA. Mass is the exception: equations use the kilogram, so turn grams into kilograms. A kilowatt-hour is energy, not power: $1$ kWh $= 1000$ W $\times 3600$ s $= 3\,600\,000$ J.

resources.title: Circuit symbols
resources.summary: The fourteen circuit symbols AQA lists, each drawn and labelled with what the component does, coloured by family: power, switches, meters, resistors, and parts that light up or work one way.

applications.title: Reading a wiring diagram
applications.body: Engineers draw circuits, from a doorbell to a car, with agreed standard symbols like these, so anyone trained to read them can build the circuit from the diagram. A few symbols differ between countries: American diagrams often draw a resistor as a zigzag.

applications.title: Automatic street lights
applications.body: A street light that switches on at dusk uses an LDR: as the light fades its resistance rises, and the circuit uses that change to turn the lamp on.

applications.title: Thermostats and fire alarms
applications.body: A thermistor’s resistance falls as it warms, so a heating controller or a heat alarm reads the temperature from the current through it.

visual.alt: Fourteen circuit symbols on tiles in two columns: cell, battery, open and closed switch, fuse, ammeter, voltmeter, resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, lamp, diode and LED, each named with what it does and coloured by family

blocks.body: **Drawing them in the exam.** Use a ruler for the wires and join them at right angles. An ammeter goes **in series**, in the loop itself; a voltmeter goes **in parallel**, across the component it measures. The long line of a cell is its **positive** side.

resources.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
resources.summary: The seven groups of electromagnetic waves in order, from radio waves to gamma rays, with the uses the specification lists for each and the harm the three with the highest frequencies can do.

applications.title: Your phone uses three of them
applications.body: It talks to the mast and to Wi-Fi with microwaves. Its camera records visible light. Its face unlock often shines infrared at you.

applications.title: Hospitals
applications.body: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are mostly absorbed by bone, which is how an X-ray image shows a fracture. Gamma rays from a carefully aimed source destroy cancer cells in radiotherapy.

applications.title: Sun cream
applications.body: The SPF on a bottle measures protection from ultraviolet, the part of sunlight that ages skin and raises the risk of skin cancer.

visual.alt: The electromagnetic spectrum as seven rows from radio waves at the top to gamma rays at the bottom, each with a wave drawn shorter than the last, its typical wavelength, its uses, and for ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays the harm they can do

blocks.body:
**Remember the order.** A common mnemonic is *Rich Men In Vegas Use eXpensive Gadgets*: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. All seven travel at the same speed in a vacuum, $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, so by $v = f\lambda$ a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency. For example, green light of wavelength $5 \times 10^{-7}$ m has frequency $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{5 \times 10^{-7}} = 6 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

**Ionising** means the radiation carries enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. That can damage the DNA in a cell, which is how X-rays and gamma rays cause mutations and cancer.

resources.title: Required practicals
resources.summary: The ten required practicals in AQA Physics: what each investigates, what you change and what you measure. Two are Physics only, not in Combined Science.

blocks.title: The ten required practicals
rows: the energy supplied, by heating a metal block for longer

the block’s mass $m$, the heater’s current and potential difference, the time and the temperature rise $\Delta\theta$. Energy supplied $\Delta E = V\,I\,t$; then $c = \dfrac{\Delta E}{m\,\Delta\theta}$. Example: a 30 W heater on for 600 s supplies $30 \times 600 = 18\,000$ J. If a 1 kg block warms by 20 °C, $c = \dfrac{18\,000}{1 \times 20} = 900$ J/kg °C.
the insulating material, or its thickness
how fast a beaker of hot water cools
the length of a wire; resistors in series and in parallel
the current and the potential difference (pd); then $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$
the potential difference (pd) across a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor
the current through each, to plot an I–V graph
the object: a regular solid, an irregular solid, then a liquid
mass on a balance; volume from length × width × height, from the water an object displaces, or from a measuring cylinder; then $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$
the force on a spring, by adding masses
the length of the spring each time. Extension = new length − original length
the force at constant mass, then the mass at constant force
the time to travel marked distances, to calculate the acceleration
the type of wave: water waves in a ripple tank, then waves on a stretched string
the frequency and the wavelength; then $v = f\,\lambda$ gives the speed
the surface, or the substance the light enters
the angles of incidence, reflection and refraction
the surface: shiny black, matt black, shiny silver, matt white
how much infrared it gives out or absorbs
blocks.note: AQA says questions drawing on these count for at least 15% of the marks. Practicals 1 to 5 belong to Paper 1 topics: energy, electricity and the particle model. Practicals 6 to 10 belong to Paper 2 topics: forces and waves. Know the method, the variables and what could go wrong with each.

applications.title: Choosing loft insulation
applications.body: Practical 2 is how a manufacturer compares insulating materials: the one that lets hot water cool slowest keeps a house warm for the least money.

applications.title: Crash testing
applications.body: Practical 7 is Newton’s second law measured. Car makers fit sensors called accelerometers inside a crash dummy. From the acceleration and the dummy’s mass, $F = m\,a$ gives the force: a 75 kg dummy slowing at 300 m/s² feels $75 \times 300 = 22\,500$ N.
